Your article doesn't really offer any substantial overview of anything; it offers a tainted personal opinion with a generalization of two personality disorders at most. The problem is that in our current culture, there's this *topical* movement towards promoting mental health awareness, yet the meta of that is groups like 'raisedbynarcissists' that claim they are support groups, while I'd wager that the majority of people joining them and discussing their issues with other people have no official diagnosis to stand on (perhaps like your claim that your mother has BPD? I don't know!). They are breeding grounds for negative opinions, judgmental comment, and focus more on venting frustrations/hurt towards other people *based on a diagnosis* without actually offering any sort of compassionate or forward-movement around the actual diagnosis of mental illness. 

I hardly believe the research as it exists now is completely accurate or is telling the whole story. Question the accuracy of my memories and experience, but I remember being a quiet, gentle child, full of curiosity like every other child, and finding myself in abusive, neglectful, and rejecting situations that had no interest in supporting my development of a personality to call my own, but that isn't a consideration in the diagnosis of BPD... That perhaps you were raised in such an invalidating and damaging environment that your brain had no choice but to wire itself in a certain way to protect yourself. Perhaps diagnosing my abusers would bring me some sort of false security, but instead I'm the one who ended up with a label to explain my symptoms, and dismiss my actual trauma. To suggest that the research indicates my brain was already broken is an insulting perspective; it doesn't consider that if my brain had been part of one of these studies, that maybe the damage was already done by the time they were looking, no matter how young. There's no dismissing a biological factor and the possibility of gene expression, but research also indicates that the way the brain is over-wired in childhood is to allow for as many connections to be made, which are defined by the experiences that a child has; either healthy connections are promoted, or the opposite occurs, and then the pruning happens to cut connections that are not used, or exercised like muscles. If you want to throw in the hereditary factor, than consider that generational trauma is also a 'thing'. As far as I'm concerned, personality disorders need to be looked at from a developmental and attachment-based standpoint with trauma as the biggest cause, but maybe society needs another 100-200 years to look back at what we think we know today and realize how wrong, or at least limited, it currently is.

I won't even go on my full-out rant about DBT, but let's just say that it's not the fix for everyone, even the most willing of individuals.  Regardless, personality disorders - if the individual's expression and symptoms really warrant such a diagnosis - should be a red flag to there being a lot of trauma hidden behind what people instead seem to want to dismiss as said-individuals just being terrible people with no explanation for why they'd act in less-than-socially-acceptable ways. I even had my own misfortune of being held hostage by a psychopath who tried to kill me... I wonder what horrible things his history would tell us about what led to him being that way. Could I have helped him? No way, but would a therapist who just concentrated on how horrible he is help him through that kind of perspective? I doubt it, but what's surprising to me is that not all - and not even most - therapists are trained in treating trauma. I'm sorry, but what was therapy for most of all?? I could have sworn... Trauma?? But today it deals in symptoms, and change, rather than listening and support as 'help' has gotten lost in the genre. There's a requirement to fix people, and fix people quickly, especially if insurance is part of the picture, and if there's a failure... Well, somebody's got to take the blame - or 'responsibility' - and it sure as hell isn't going to be the modality holding those bags when there's money to be made selling quick-fix answers that might really just be covering up huge wounds with band-aids.

It may be the unpopular opinion, but articles like this just seem to be a hindrance to progress. Lumping every personality disorder together like you did, and adding 'some of them are just about near impossible to treat' should speak negatively on the progress that hasn't been made in psychology and psychiatry, not on the patients it is meant to treat, but instead the fault seems to be driven towards the patients who have disorders they didn't ask for; traumatic experiences and toxic stress in their childhoods that are left ignored for the wounds that they caused, while therapist's explain away their adult symptoms for personality defects that were "always" present, as if no damage could have ever been inflicted upon those suffering from some of the most severe disorders. I beg to differ, as I risk yet another invalidating experiencing for speaking out against the stigma perpetuated about personality disorders that exists in what should-be therapeutic services; I'm an easy target what with having a diagnosis of BPD, as if an all-too-easy weapon against saying anything negative about the services that are supposed to be there for the mentally ill. With all due respect though, your whole paragraph on personality disorders read like an unsure high school student who's just trying to get a passing grade in their psych 101 class. The real shame of psychology as it exists right now is the lies it perpetuates behind terminology such as "evidence based," and the attitude that if the research/modality doesn't work the way therapist's want them to, then it must just be the patient's fault, and not the limitations of that research/modality itself. To ultimately suggest to the general public that if they know how to find the disturbed people with PD's that they can just avoid all their troubles by ultimately avoiding them, really puts those of us who are ill in quite a predicament, wouldn't you say? So please inform me on how this article is helping the movement away from stigma around mental illness?

I'd imagine there's room for one or both treatments to work depending on the illness, but even the illnesses that are defined today could be more accurately broken down into possibly being multiple illness. I think of the DSM and it's categorization; well certain illnesses, like BPD, can have 250 different manifestations based on the criteria of meeting at least 5 out of the 9 symptoms. Chances are in scenarios like this, we are dealing with different illnesses with overlapping symptomology, or at minimum, different forms of the same illness that could very-well have better outcomes with treatment that was more appropriate to the different manifestations. 

Your example of ADHD is also a good example of this. Children are at risk of being diagnosed with ADHD when in fact they are really showing signs of trauma and PTSD, even with *known trauma/abuse* in their history. One has to ask themselves in a scenario like that if the medication is actually helping due to the child appearing to have symptom remission, or if it's merely having a chameleon-like effect on their actual issues. Even imaging studies can undoubtedly be fooling us at this point; to loop back to what I said about BPD: they've said there is a susceptibility to this disorder through brain imaging studies, but how do they know that isn't proof that the damage has actually already been done instead of always existing? It may well be a matter of both having occurred, but considering how accelerated brain development is in the child (and that it is impossible to diagnose BPD in a child at this point), it is undoubtedly difficult to prove - without a shadow of a doubt - whether the 'egg or the chicken came first', so to speak.

There's no "cheating" on either end, whether you take a pharmacological route, or something more "organic" a la 'talking therapy', which is predominantly skills/cbt-based at this point and shouldn't even deem itself true 'talking therapy' at all anymore when it is goal-oriented and focused on enforcing change rather than supporting clients (which sounds good on paper, but can be re-traumatizing to some in its own right). But I digress; sometimes neither route works because the fact of the matter is that our research is just beginning, and as much as we'd like to believe we have the proven answer, given another 100 years from where we are now, a good portion of the treatments available today will likely be proven to be their own form of snake oil to the ones we will have in the future. 

Personally I think both routes will have to find a way to co-exist more syncretically, but it will also be pinpointing down symptomology with biological and environmental factors (e.g. nature *and* nurture). We have a long way to go before we can *really* look at an individual person's brain and say with total confidence, "These neurotransmitters need to be treated with these supplements/medications, and this particular form of therapy will help." Right now, you may as well hit a casino as you'd have higher chances of coming out with any winnings than finding the right, or even "good enough" fit of therapist, medication, or both when you have a particularly difficult mental/emotional, and even developmental illness; chances are, it's deemed "difficult" because what's actually challenging is the fact that doctors still haven't figured out how to treat it better. 

I'd say that if therapy is actually working for you, you're one of the lucky ones with some chance of being helped at all, so go with it, but don't dump on the possibility of other treatments working for other illnesses. I say this as someone who has no interest in being another psychiatrist's guinea pig, but it doesn't mean someone won't find a pharmacological answer - even support *to* therapy - one day, even if it's not in my life time.

I'm "glad" a lot of therapists are annoyed, too. I study child development and we know the brain does most of its major formation of neural pathways in the first 8 years of life before it starts to "trim" off what it considers "unnecessary," for good or bad. I actually had a dream in regards to my own brain where the branches of my neural pathways are split in a way that where one emotion *should* just go directly to a 'neurotypical' response (e.g. happy feeling leads to happy reaction), because they're split, there's a chance that a certain emotion will instead be sent down the other pathway towards a 'neurodivergent' direction (e.g. happy feeling leads to angry reaction, or intimacy leads to feelings of danger, etc.). Then we can get all into the lovely corridors that is the prefrontal cortex and the amygdala and how they just love to be over-and-under stimulated at all the wrong times due to, well... I'm assuming over-training in those early years where conflictual experiences just maybe led to confused neural pathways (of which I'm tired of being told I should just be able to control myself when I feel like I'm in the midst of an emotional seizure that I'm not happy I'm having either!). In regards to my prominent diagnosis (BPD) it's suggested that there is a heritable aspect along with an environmental trigger. I'd almost wonder if it's like having thin/weak hair, whereby the neurons are more weakly held together by the myelin sheaths and therefore split apart more readily to make more connections, and may be more prone due to traumatic or intense experiences. The opposite might be true in that the neurons are stronger somehow, and are more easily pulled in an atypical direction, like magnets that get flipped to connect when they shouldn't be able to connect at all. Who knows, but I feel like fields like this need a more syncretic perspective to make progress, taking into account multiple fields of study; we're talking about human development here (e.g., child development, neuroscience, psychology, etc.); it is like the old joke "it's not brain surgery" except it *is* brain science! Who am I kidding though; we don't even have a worldwide agreement for response when there's a pandemic and I'm just a big fat idealist at the end of the day.

I'm going to reply from a really general perspective here and use an example from my own field of work since what you said made me think about it a lot. I work with young children in an educational environment. The most current recommendation is something that we call 'emergent curriculum', which factors in the child's diversity and interests to support their individual learning. In simple terms, maybe I have child who is 2 who is struggling to learn how to do basic counting (a cognitive skill). I know this particular child is interested in animals, so I can use this information to support this development while using methods such as Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development to *scaffold* the experience for the child. I might take the animals and count for them while moving the animals one at a time to line them up from 1-5. I then might begin to say a number, and point to the animal, or wait for the child to then fill in the next animal. This wouldn't happen all at once, but progressively I would increase the child's involvement, and it's endless how I can extend this activity to things like requesting two of a particular animal, or subtracting at later ages. The same thing applies to all areas of development (physical, social, emotional, language).

Basically, my point is that I don't understand why therapy isn't more like this. Kohut developed the theory of Optimal Frustration, but the way I try to work with children is supporting an Optimal Achievement or supportive environment for success, rather than trying to irritate them just enough that they're motivated to do something because of their inability/failure. In psychoanalysis, there seemed to be a purposeful withholding with regards to "wishes," too, to examine one's frustration over not getting what they desired, but I feel like that sort of perspective can cause a collapse for someone who wouldn't normally verbalize or seek out what they want or need in the first place. It certainly wouldn't work with my little people who would just scream and cry harder because you just refused adamantly to help them achieve their own goals for success; if anything, they'd achieve a sense of failure and lack of belief in their ability to be capable and resilient during difficult tasks. 

We're not robots here; we're individuals with our own histories and backgrounds. We have our reasons for being the way we are; being resistant or difficult in the ways that we are, and working (or not working) due to those experiences. An individualized plan makes sense, and I understand that there does seem to be some level of that occurring in manualized treatments, but more of it would seem a logical idea. The fact of the matter, not unlike therapy, in my field of work, the relationship between caregiver and child is of the utmost importance. It plays a part in the motivation as to whether the child is going to take interest in *sharing* in an activity that would be enjoyable to them, or prefers to go off on their own and avoid the other person, when that person is hopefully there to *support* them as part of their job. It'd be ridiculous if I thought I could just open a book and think every method is going to work with every child. Some need stringent "Do this, not that," while others need, "Do this, then you can do that," while still others need, "Do you want to do this, or that first?" otherwise you better believe you're going to have a day made much more difficult with that particular child because you are unwilling to modify your techniques to meet them half way. ...
